title: Sumerian cities, writing and accounts
summary: Sumer matters not because one claim of being first can explain every complex society, but because cities concentrated many capabilities. Temples, storage, crafts, trade and administration depended on one another. Competing and cooperating city-states together formed a connected world.

blocks.text: Sumer matters not because one claim of being first can explain every complex society, but because cities concentrated many capabilities. Temples, storage, crafts, trade and administration depended on one another. Competing and cooperating city-states together formed a connected world.

Southern Mesopotamian cities exchanged resources with agricultural hinterlands and obtained timber, stone and metals from elsewhere. Irrigation maintenance demanded internal organization, while raw materials encouraged distant exchange. Cities faced coordination at home and dependence abroad from the outset.

As movements of food, labor and goods became more complex, records became more valuable. Writing and accounts made collection, distribution and responsibility easier to preserve and trace. They were closely connected to practical problems of urban administration.

Writing therefore needs to be understood alongside institutions. Records require trained writers, purposes and organizations that maintain their use. Sumer illustrates a dense combination of mutually supporting capabilities, rather than one invention independently creating a civilization.
